> good point...
>
> here is how to do this.
>
> Poisson(exp(eta) * s)
>
> where s ~ Gamma(1/delta,1/delta)
>

>

> choice is lambda=7. the initial value is just the starting value.
>
> lambda = 7
> n = 10^6
> delta = inla.pc.rgamma(n, lambda = lambda)
> s = rgamma(n, shape = 1/delta,  rate = 1/delta)
> hist(s,  n = 100)
>
> hope this helps!
> H

messages.subject: Posteriors for derived parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I feel like I should know the answer to this question, but I don't.  I am wondering about the best way to calculate credible intervals for derived parameters from a model when using INLA.  For example, I have three populations of snakes.  I want to estimate body mass for each population given an average body length.  I have an ANCOVA, with a centered length covariate, an intercept to estimate mean mass and credible interval for population A, and two other estimates and credible intervals for differences between populations A and B, and A and C.  I understand that I just add the posterior means for differences between groups to the posterior mean of the intercept to get the posterior mean masses for populations B and C.  But how do I get a credible intervals for mean masses of populations B and population C, when they are derived from two sets of posteriors?  If I were doing this with MCMC, I'd calculate a derived mass for each population at each iteration to get a posterior for each population mass.  But what is the best way to get this using INLA?  Some code and output -- and question marks -- below.

###   make data  ###
n.groups <- 3; n.sample <- 30
n <- n.groups * n.sample
x <- rep(1:n.groups, rep(n.sample, n.groups))
pop <- factor(x, labels = c("Population A", "Population B", "Population C"))
length <- runif(n, 45, 70)
Xmat <- model.matrix(~ pop*length)
print(Xmat, dig = 2)
beta.vec <- c(-250, 150, 200, 6, -3, -4)
lin.pred <- Xmat[,] %*% beta.vec
eps <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 0, sd = 10)
mass <- lin.pred + eps
dat <- data.frame(mass=mass, pop=pop, length=length)
dat$length <- scale(dat$length)
library(lattice); xyplot(mass ~ length | pop, data=dat)

###  inla model  ###
library(INLA)
form <- mass ~ pop + length
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat))

### output  ###
Fixed effects:      mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode kld
(Intercept)     103.7029 2.6876    98.3992 103.7078   108.9734 103.7175   0
popPopulation B -29.1395 3.8482   -36.6901 -29.1472   -21.5547 -29.1619   0
popPopulation C -29.5663 3.7750   -36.9742 -29.5736   -22.1265 -29.5874   0
length           23.5600 1.5984    20.4108  23.5611    26.6996  23.5634   0

Model hyperparameters:       mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode
Precision for the Gaussian 0.0047 7e-04     0.0035   0.0047     0.0061 0.0046

### means and credible intervals ###
Mean mass for population A is 103.7 (98.4, 109.0)
Mean mass for population B is 103.7 - 29.1 = 74.6 (?, ?)
Mean mass for population C is 103.7 - 29.6 = 74.1 (?, ?)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posteriors for derived parameters
messages.body_plain:
If all you need are linear combinations of the latent variables (that looks like the case in your example) you can use the lincomb feature. See the FAQ on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> and the general documentation.

For more complex and/or nonlinear functionals, you can obtain posterior samples inla.posterior.sample() (which does direct MC sampling, not MCMC).

Finn

messages.subject: changes in 'rgeneric'
messages.body_plain:
This post is related to the 'rgeneric' tool, see inla.doc("rgeneric"),
for which we had to make some changes to that are not backward
compatible, so if you use this you need to update your code.

the problem was to make rgeneric 'thread safe', in the sense that you
can have several rgeneric models and they will not interfer with each
other even though they share the same .GlobalEnv and 'R-session'

inla.doc("rgeneric")  shows the new use. in short. there are no longer
any constant arguments passed into the rgeneric function, and such ones
are now  set in the environment attached to the function.

it seems that the usage is as before, like

model = inla.rgeneric.define(fun, n=73, shape=3, rate=2)

but 'n', 'shape' and 'rate' will now be assigned in fun's environment
so they  are accessible from within 'fun' (this is done automatic).

hence, 'fun' now reads like

inla.rgeneric.de <http://inla.rgeneric.de>`inla.rgeneric.ar1.model` = function(
        cmd = c("graph", "Q", "mu", "initial", "log.norm.const",
                "log.prior", "quit"),
        theta = NULL)
{
    graph = function(){ <to be completed> }
    Q = function() { <to be completed> }
	....

    val = do.call(match.arg(cmd), args = list())
    return (val)
}

note, no arguments any more to internal functions, and hence the
'args=list()' argument in 'do.call'

'theta' is already defined, whereas the others, 'n', 'shape', 'rate'
are there already in the fun's environment, so that

	dgamma(exp(theta[1]), rate=rate, shape=shape)

will do the right thing.

as a consequence, the argument 'R.init' is removed, and you have to
pass precomputed stuff as argument(s) in 'inla.rgeneric.define', so
they will be defined in the fun's environment, and you can access them
from within 'fun'.

sorry about this, but it was required. this is still an experimental
feature, though...

H

--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posteriors for derived parameters
messages.body_plain:
Here is the code for solution to example for anyone interested. Thanks again, Finn!

### Linear combinations - simple ANCOVA example
### Make data

n.groups <- 3
n.sample <- 30
n <- n.groups * n.sample
x <- rep(1:n.groups, rep(n.sample, n.groups))
pop <- factor(x, labels = c("Population A", "Population B",

                            "Population C")) ### Categorical factor
length <- runif(n, 45, 70) ### Continuous covariate

Xmat <- model.matrix(~ pop*length)
print(Xmat, dig = 2)
beta.vec <- c(-250, 150, 200, 6, -3, -4)
lin.pred <- Xmat[,] %*% beta.vec
eps <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 0, sd = 10)
mass <- lin.pred + eps
dat <- data.frame(mass=mass, pop=pop, length=length)

dat$length <- scale(dat$length, scale=F) # note that length is centered
library(lattice); xyplot(mass ~ length | pop, data=dat) ### Plot of data

### simple ANCOVA model without linear combinations

library(INLA)
form <- mass ~ pop + length
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat))

### Create linear combinations to get posteriors for masses of Populations
##### B and C at average length
### NOTE that NAMES of EFFECTS can be gleaned from fixed effects output of
##### previous model. Just need to set the desired values for each effect.
lcPopB <- inla.make.lincomb("(Intercept)"=1, "popPopulation B"=1,
             "popPopulation C"=0, length=0)
lcPopC <- inla.make.lincomb("(Intercept)"=1, "popPopulation B"=0,
             "popPopulation C"=1, length=0)
lcAllPop <- c(lcPopB, lcPopC) ### Combine into a group
names(lcAllPop) <- c("lcPopB","lcPopC") ### MUST give unique names to each

### Rerun the model with the linear combinations
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat,
                    ### Add the linear combinations here
                    lincomb = lcAllPop,
                    ### Force noise variance to be essentially zero
                    control.family = list(initial=10, fixed=TRUE),
                    ### For higher accuracy
                    control.inla = list(lincomb.derived.only=FALSE)))

### Access summary of linear combinations
res$summary.lincomb

### Plot posteriors for mass of each population
yx <- data.frame(rbind(res$marginals.fixed$"(Intercept)",
                       res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopB,
                       res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopC))
yx$poplab <- rep(c("Population A", "Population B",  "Population C"),
                 each=nrow(res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopC))
xyplot(y~x|poplab, yx, scales=list(relation="free"), type="l",
       xlab="Posterior mass for each population", ylab="Density")

### Done

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Sorry I should have given more detail. These are observed (response variable) vs predicted posterior median plots. Eexp(linear.predictor) is the transformed median of the linear predictor as you guessed, and fitted.values refers to the median from summary.fitted.values.

The red line is the 1-to-1 line, and the blue line is a simple linear regression. Ideally the blue line would match the fixed red line and that would indicate an unbiased model fit/forecast. However the posterior medians are systematically larger than the observed values (response variable), indicated by the downward skew.

I am interested in adjusting the prior for size to try and account for the high overdispersion. In the INLA negative binomial documentation it states that the prior for size is pc.mgamma and is defined on theta, given

size = E*exp(theta)

However when I try to adjust the initial values for this prior using

control.family = list(variant = 1, hyper = list(theta = list(prior = "pc.mgamma", params = c(...

I get an error saying pc.mgamma is unknown? Should I use loggamma instead?

Thanks,
Hayden

On 28 February 2017 at 15:09, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> What _precisely_ is "Eexp(linear.predictor)" in the plots? If it's the transformed medians of the linear predictor, and the lines in the plots labeled fitted.values are the medians of the fitted.values, then yes, there is a discrepancy, and they also both differ from the blue lines. The discrepancy may very well be due to what Håvard mentioned about the high overdispersion causing numerical issues, or similar. The apparent overprediction (assuming the blue line is objectively better) I don't have an explanation for (unless you're fitting a different model in the blue and red cases).
>

> >
> > The clear over prediction occurs with all model specifications (the results below are from the best model - test R-squared of 0.255).

> >
> > <image.png>

> > Could this be due to over estimation of the size parameter for the negative binomial distribution? Should I define stricter hyper-parameters on the pc.mgamma prior for size?
> >
> >
> > Thanks again for all the help,
> > Hayden

> > On 28 February 2017 at 11:36, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > On 27 Feb 2017, at 20:05, Hayden Rabel <hayden...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Should E(exp(summary.linear.predictor)) be equivalent to summary.fitted.values in this case? I am finding slight discrepancies between these two vectors.
> > >
> > > Hi,
> > >  adding a few comments to what Håvard mentioned:
> > > Yes, in theory the expectation (mean) in summary.fitted.values should be the same as E(exp(linearpredictor)), since they are calculated in different ways, there will always be numerical discrepancies. When you say "slight", precisely what do you mean? Anything that's much smaller than the width of the quantile based prediction interval is ignorable. If the difference is a noticeable fraction of that, then there might be cause for concern.
> > >
> > > Precisely how are you assessing the posteriors? What kind of residuals? Because expectations and link functions are not commutative, E(g(x)) is not g(E(x)), one always needs to be extremely careful in comparing like-for-like.  If you only use the quantiles of the inla output, and no expectations and variances, and evaluate only such prediction intervals, do you still see what you called overprediction?  There might still be issues with highly dispersed distributions, but quantiles are at least much more stable, in theory, than expectations and variances.
> > >
> > > If your need to assess point estimates, perhaps the posterior medians are more useful that the posterior means?  Those should be assessed using e.g. mean absolute deviation of the residuals.
> > >
> > > Finn L

> > > >
> > > > When using exp(E(summary.linear.predictor)) the over-prediction mentioned previously is inflated even further?

messages.subject: Error in !scale.model : invalid argument type
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

When using 'BYM' or "Besag" models, I keep getting the error message for "Error in !scale.model : invalid argument type". It seems like I can create a graph for the spatial locations but "BYM" models doesn't accept it.

The following is my code. Did I do anything wrong?

Thanks a lot,

Xintong Li

library(spdep)   # a big library of spatial functions

library(INLA)
### read shape file
nepal<-readShapePoly('/Users/xintongli/Downloads/NP_75DWGS84/NP_75DWGS84.shp')

deaths<-read.csv("/Users/xintongli/Downloads/NepalDeath.csv")

nepal.sort<-nepal[order(nepal$DISTRICT),]

deaths.sort<-deaths[order(deaths$Districts),]

deaths.sort$DistID<-1:39

match<-nepal.sort$DISTRICT%in%deaths.sort$Districts

nepal.hasmap<-nepal.sort[match,]

#nepal.hasmap$DISTRICT==deaths.sort$Districts

#plot(nepal.hasmap)

# Define neighborhood method 1
neighbor<-poly2nb(nepal.hasmap)

#convert to INLA neighborhood format and store in dropbox
nb2INLA("/Users/xintongli/Downloads/nepaldistrict.graph",neighbor)

district.adj=("/Users/xintongli/Downloads/nepaldistrict.graph")

# read in INLA graph
H <- inla.read.graph(filename=district.adj)

# plot an image of INLA graph
image(inla.graph2matrix(H)

formula1<-Death ~ 1+ f(DistID, model='besag',graph = district.adj, constr=TRUE)

model <- inla(Death ~ 1+ f(DistID, model='besag',graph = district.adj, constr=TRUE), family="Gaussian",
              data=deaths.sort,
              control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
              control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

round(model$summary.fixed[,1:5],3)
model$dic$dic

messages.subject: inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed problem with Besag model
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA members,

   I am building a model where I am trying to use 'Besag' model for  one spatial component that is connected to observation with a projector matrix (Foot). I have one other spatial component (modeled with 'Besag' model) that has no projector matrix. I have the projector matrix from atmospheric model, and two adjacency matrices that I have created.

Here are few details of the model:

# length(y)
# 300
# dim(Foot)  :Big projector matrix in sparse format
# 300 15480
#dim(stateAdj)  :Big adjacency matrix for first spatial component in sparse format (binary with 1 in diagonal)
#15480 15480
#dim(ycor_adj) :Adjacency matrix for second spatial component in sparse format (binary with 1 in diagonal)
# 300 300
# sum(adj_mat[adj_mat==1])/{ncol(adj_mat)}^2
# 0.000887692  :the matrix seems quite sparse

## model

stk.e <- inla.stack(tag='est', ## tag
                    data=list(y=y), ## response
                    A=list(Foot, 1, 1), ## two projector matrices
                    effects=list(## two elements:
                      s1=1:ncol(Foot), ## RF index
                      s2=1:nrow(Foot), ## RF index
                      data.frame(x=HX)))

formula <- y ~ 0 + x + ## fixed part
  f(s1, model='besag',graph=stateAdj,adjust.for.con.comp = FALSE,
    scale.model=TRUE) + ## RF term
  f(s2, model='besag',graph=ycor_adj,scale.model=TRUE)

INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()   # otherwise it was showing errors and I found this fix from this group**
inla.setOption(num.threads=2)
#control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian")

res <- inla(formula,
            data=inla.stack.data(stk.e),
            control.predictor=list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.e),compute=TRUE),
            quantiles=NULL,
            control.results=list(return.marginals.random=FALSE,
            return.marginals.predictor=FALSE),
            verbose=TRUE)    # projector

####

I am running it in cluster with 1 node - 32gb memory (16 cores) where R (3.2.3) is built with IntelMKL. Problem I encounter is whatever number of threads I use or whatever strategy I choose, it throws me the error (or something very similar) that:

 taucs_calloc_stub fail to calloc 167236624 elements of size 8 bytes
 Aborted (core dumped)
 Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
 The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.

If  I run a simple model with only the smaller spatial component, then it works. But, first spatial component is actually the integral part for this problem. I read almost all the other related threads but I couldn't seem to fix it. Could you please help?

Thanks,
Subhomoy

messages.body_plain:
Dear Rue,

     Sure. Attached here is a zip file containing the R code I pasted and the data. Just wanted to mention that the way I create these adjacency matrices and projector matrix are the following:

    Projector matrix: Foot comes from atmospheric models. These are influence functions or sensitivities of the observation w.r.t gridded emission fields (the big spatial field in the model- # grids 15480 -- a 120*129 domain). Projector * emission + RF + Errors are basically observations.

  Adjacency matrix of the emission field (first spatial field): I compute this based on nearest neighbor of several spatial layer (roads,urban layer,power plants, others) that constitutes the emission field. I know coordinates of each layer. For each layer, I compute a k-nearest neighbor based adjacency matrix and then I plug them in the 15480*15480 matrix based on their relative coordinate indices. Lastly I just make it binary.

 2nd adjacency is simple and based on a criteria on the correlation matrix of an ensemble of observations (300*300).

Hope this helps.

Thanks,
Subhomoy

Foot = inla.as.sparse(Foot)
for(i in 1:nrow(Foot)) {
    v = Foot[i, ]
    v[abs(v) < max(abs(v))*0.01] = 0
    Foot[i, ] = v

}

the reason is here:

	Size of graph=[30603] constraints=[3]

row, which is insanely many elements...

this is why it takes time (and use so much memory)

can you do anything (more) about this?

H

messages.body_plain:
I second Haakon's suggestion, and add another note:

In a spatial model, the posterior standard deviations themselves (and certainly the posterior precision matrices, so any $config output used for posterior samples for example) can reveal the locations of the data; if the data points are scattered and isolated, one can reverse-engineer them, since the posterior precision matrix is essentially of the form Q+A' Qe A, where Q and Qe are determined by the estimated model parameters (and therefore known) and A encodes the data locations. The diagonal of the precision, or the diagonal of its inverse (the posterior variances) are enough to locate isolated data locations. You'll have to decide whether this is a realistic enough risk in your situation.

This general problem is seeing a lot more research now, but I don't think I've seen anyone specifically address this version of the issue.

Finn

messages.subject: (mild) regularity conditions
messages.body_plain:
Good evening,

I am new to R-INLA and novice in statistics. I was reading papers about INLA and they all state that, to use INLA, "(mild) regularity conditions" have to be met, but do not go into details about what it means.
It is probably obvious to everyone here, but what does this mean? Does it have anything to do with making sure the precision matrix is positive definite? And how do I know if a function not listed in the latent models could meet those conditions?

Thank you very much for your help.

If it is something too long/complicated to explain on this board, I would appreciate a reference to this as I have googled this for hours and could not find an answer.
Again, thank you.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] (mild) regularity conditions
messages.body_plain:
you can check this one,

http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047259X12001297

and the intuition behind the approximations (which kind of say what
conditions you need to make them work),

https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00860

or here, if you have access

http://www.annualreviews.org/journal/statistics

I would not worry to much. one need log likelihoods to be continous,
and two times derivative, preferably concave, and similar conditions
for the log priors.

H

messages.subject: posterior of joint (misalignment) model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to help here and from Xavi Barber I've created a model for misaligned data. When I predict from the posterior mean of this joint model, though, the values seem to be on a very different scale than they are in a non-misaligned model, and it looks like I'm basically just predicting the mesh structure.

Here is most of the model prep. stk.x is from a point dataset with 19,000 points, stk.y is a different dataset with 2000 misaligned points that I hypothesize predict the distribution of x. Both are binomial. I have this id term in the stk.x stack just because it wasn't happy with me listing only the spatial field, but the id term isn't used in the model.

> A.x <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = loc_x)
> A.y <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = loc_y)
> A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = p.coords)
>
> stk.x <- inla.stack(tag='est.x',
+                     data=list(y=cbind(data$result, NA)),
+                     A=list(A.x, 1),
+                     effects=list(xi.field=1:spde2$n.spde,
+                                  id=data$id))
>
> stk.y <- inla.stack(data=list(y=cbind(NA, cmv$result)),
+                     A = list(A.y, 1),
+                     tag ='est.y',
+                     effects=list(list(u.field=1:spde2$n.spde,
+                                       x.field=1:spde2$n.spde),
+                                  list(intercept = rep(1, length(cmv$result)))))
> grid$na1<-NA
> grid$na2<-NA
> NAgrid<-as.matrix(cbind(grid$na1, grid$na2))
> stk.p <- inla.stack(tag='prediction',
+                          data=list(y=NAgrid),
+                          A=list(A.pred, 1),
+                          effects=list(list(s=1:spde2$n.spde),
+                          list(intercept = rep(1, length(grid$id)))))
>
> stk <- inla.stack.join(stk.x, stk.y, stk.p)
>
> form_mis <- y ~ -1 + intercept +
+   f(xi.field, model=spde2) +
+   f(x.field, model=spde2) +
+   f(u.field, copy='xi.field', fixed=FALSE)
>
> model_mis <- inla(form_mis, data=inla.stack.data(stk), family=rep('binomial',2),
+                   control.predictor=list(compute=FALSE, A=inla.stack.A(stk)),
+                   control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config=TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
+                   verbose = TRUE)

The image shown below is from:

m.prd<-model_mis$summary.fitted.values[inla.stack.index(stk, "prediction")$data,"mean"]

The coordinates for the prediction stack are a regular grid covering the whole study area.

Obviously there's very little variability in the range of m.prd, but it's also completely different than when I predict from a simple model (not incorporating the misaligned predictor). When I run a simpler model with just stk.x by itself, the posterior mean values are in the 0.02 to 0.05 range. What I really want to learn from this model is if the variability in stk.y accounts for the variability in stk.x, i.e. does the variability in x decrease when y is added to the model.

messages.body_plain:
Quick reply:
You don't seem to use the link argument that tells inla to apply the link function for the fitted.values calculations.
In the data arguments to the stacks, use link=1 in the one with data in the first column, and link=2 for the one with data in the second column.for the predictions, specify whichever of the two you want (in your case both are binomial, so it doesn't matter which one, as long as you do specify something).

Then supply link=inla.stack.data(stk)$link in the control.predictor argument list.

Finn

Since your predictions are all within a very narrow range, and your plotting code scales the colour scale to the range of the values, the mesh structure appears because that's the scale at which the small spatial variation "lives".
(There's something other strange, since on my laptop the clour scale matches the ~0.998 range, but on my tablet, it shows ~7.211; I'm suspecting some email system is doing something strange, and you initially attached the linear.predictor field plot.)

You most likely expected some structure in the estimate.  Hard to tell why that doesn't happen; it depends on the data...

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I've attached an image essentially showing two superimposed models.

The color background is the odds of hearing loss among 19,000 infants. The pointwise odds varies from 0.02 to 0.05, and the pointwise odds ratio (local vs global) varies from 0.6 to 1.4.

The contours are from a GAM of 2200 pregnant women tested for the virus CMV, which can cause infant hearing loss. These are spatially misaligned, and these are not (necessarily) the mothers of the infants in the infant dataset.

So the biological hypothesis is that the spatial variation in infant hearing loss is a function of spatial variation in maternal CMV infection.

As you can see the areas where there is significantly high odds of maternal CMV corresponds almost perfectly to areas with high infant hearing loss, and vice versa. So it shouldn't be a surprise that an effective adjustment should wipe out variability in the "dependent" variable, the infant hearing loss.

So is there a way to examine the relationship between these two point patterns in the combined model to see if this really is an "adjusted" model with a flat output -- as opposed to (more likely) some mistake I've made?

Are you sure you don't want an intercept in the x-model?
Perhaps a separate one from he y-model?
E.g intercept.x=1 here, intercept.y=1 in the stk.y, and intercept.x+intercept.y in the formula?

> +                          effects=list(list(s=1:spde2$n.spde),
> +                          list(intercept = rep(1, length(grid$id)))))

Where you have s=... I'm pretty sure you want either I.field, x.field, or u.field.
You current stack only uses the intercept, since s doesn't exist in the formula!
If you want the predictions to show the discrepancies between x and y, I think you want x.field, and _not_ apply a link function (so use link=NA in stk.p).
I think earlier discussions revealed that that would give some log-odds-ratio information, but I may be mixing up different things.

It always helps to spell out the mathematical definition of what the models and predictions are, independently of how they are specified in software, as that's the only way to check that the code implements the right thing.

Finn

> only. if you estimate missing data outsida inla, using some other
> methods, and feed these also into inla together with the observed data,
> then the DIC would use both of them.

}

Probably related to whatever's causing aa < bb below

phi = 0.05

graph = system.file(
  "demodata/germany.graph",
  package="INLA")

adjust.for.con.comp = TRUE

Q = INLA:::inla.pc.bym.Q(graph)
n = dim(Q)[1]
g = INLA:::inla.read.graph(Q)
nc = g$cc$n
rankdef = nc
log.q1.det = INLA:::inla.sparse.det.bym(Q,
  adjust.for.con.comp = adjust.for.con.comp)

constr = list(A = matrix(0, nc, n), e = rep(0, nc))
for(k in 1:nc) {
  constr$A[k, g$cc$nodes[[k]]] = 1
}

Qinv.d = diag(inla.qinv(
    Q + Diagonal(n) * max(diag(Q)) * eps,
    constr))

f = mean(Qinv.d) - 1.0

aa = n*phi*f

if (phi <= 0.5) {
  eps = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
  rdef = 0
} else {
  eps = 0
  rdef = 1
}

bb = n * log((1.0 - phi)/phi) +
  INLA:::inla.sparse.det.bym(Q + (phi/(1-phi) + eps) *
      Diagonal(n), rankdef = rdef,
    adjust.for.con.comp = adjust.for.con.comp) -
  (log.q1.det - (n-rankdef) * log(phi))

c(aa, bb)

if (aa >= bb) sqrt(aa-bb) else NA

messages.subject: Slow spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
We are using a spatiotemporal model and would very much appreciate any guidance on how to speed it up.
We have a poisson model for mortality count data at the level of year/age.group/district with 30 years, 19 age groups and 376 districts (covering England and Wales).

We would like to run the model below.
So far we have only managed to run a reduced model which excludes both of the rw1 terms (f(year3,...) and f(year5,...)), and this takes about 35 hours. This was run on a 64-bit desktop with 96Gb RAM.
However, once we add in the rw over time for each district, f(year5,..), the run time is over over 1 week - we actually terminated it so this is a lower limit on time.

I believe using "exchangeable" will mean that the hyperparameter is shared across the groups but there is no correlation between the group rw's.
We tried restarting from a "cheap" run.
Unfortunately we are not permitted to share the data.

Any help would be very much appreciated.
best
James

  fml  <- m ~
  # national terms
1 +                                                        # national intercept
year1 +                                                  # national trend

  # age specific terms
f(age1, model="iid") +                                                    # age specific intercepts
f(age2, year2 , model="iid") +                                            # age specific trends
f(year3,model="rw1",group=age3,control.group=list(model="exchangeable")) + # rw over time for each age group

  # district specific terms
f(dist1, model="besag",graph=adj) +                                              # structured district specific intercept
f(dist2, year4, model="besag",graph=adj) +                              # structured district specific trends
f(year5,model="rw1",group=dist3,control.group=list(model="exchangeable")) + # rw over time for each district

  # overdispersion term for each year/age/district
f(e, model = "iid")

  system.time(mod <-
                inla(formula = fml,
                     family = "poisson",
                     data = dat.inla,
                     E = pop,
                     control.compute = list(dic=TRUE),
#for cheap run:
#control.inla=list(int.strategy = "eb",strategy = "gaussian",diagonal=10000),
control.inla=list(diagonal=0),
control.predictor = list(link = 1),
verbose=FALSE,
#for start from cheap run of the same model:
control.mode = list( result = mod_cheap, restart = TRUE)
)
  )

Hi,

I am trying obtain a sample from the approximating joint posterior of the hyperparameters, with corresponding log-posterior values. The joint.hyper component of the inla results gives the joint log-posteriors for the grid points used in the inference, whereas I can sample hyperparameters from the approximating joint posterior using inla.hyperpar.sample function. But this does not give corresponding posterior values (which makes sense). But is there some other way to obtain similar output as from joint.hyper but with sampled points?

Best regards,
Jouni

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2017-03-28 at 04:03 -0700, Jouni Helske wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am trying obtain a sample from the approximating joint posterior of
> the hyperparameters, with corresponding log-posterior values. The
> joint.hyper component of the inla results gives the joint log-
> posteriors for the grid points used in the inference, whereas I can
> sample hyperparameters from the approximating joint posterior using
> inla.hyperpar.sample function. But this does not give corresponding
> posterior values (which makes sense). But is there some other way to
> obtain similar output as from joint.hyper but with sampled points?

Hi,

inla.hyperpar.sample()  will provide sample from the joint of \theta,
but cannot (yet) evaluate a sample. If this is an issue, it can be
fixed.

inla.posterior.sample() will provide samples fromt he joint of (\theta,
x), and can evaluate density, but will for \theta only use the
integration points.

and you need samples of \theta only with the densities?

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Slow spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I see two issues that causes an increase in the computing time in your model: the number of constraints and the lack of sparseness of the resulting precision matrix in two terms:

f(year3,model="rw1",group=age3,control.group=list(model="exchangeable")) + # rw over time for each age group

f(year5,model="rw1",group=dist3,control.group=list(model="exchangeable")) + # rw over time for each district

It needs 19 and 376 constraints, respectively, and both delivers non sparse precision as you have 'exchangeable' for the groups. You can avoid the constraints changing from 'rw1' to 'ar1' in both. You can fix the 'rho' parameter in 'ar1' near one.

You can avoid to have a dense matrix changing from 'exchangeable' to 'ar1' in the first case and to 'besagproper' in the second. These two choices for the group can be justified as you do have ordering in 'age3' and a neighborhood in 'dist3'. Notice that you can fix the 'rho' parameter in 'ar1' near one and the 'd' parameter in 'besagproper' near zero if you want, as your model has already 9 hyperparameters.

Elias

messages.subject: Unexpectedly bad results with Poisson time series
messages.subject_clean: Unexpectedly bad results with Poisson time series
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am testing INLA with simple Poisson time series models, and got some surprising results. As a latent states x, I simulated Gaussian AR(1) process and generated my observations as a Poisson(exp(x)). The autoregressive parameter tends to estimate fine, but sigma/tau is way off. I'll attach a document which illustrates the issue and compares the results with Stan.

I have tried to check the prior definitions etc but I can't see any problems in the model specifications. I know that binomial models with small counts can be problematic with INLA but is this common phenomenon in Poisson models as well, or am I doing something wrong?

Best regards,

Jouni

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another crash problem
messages.body_plain:
Further to Daniel's question of what your stacks are intended to do:
1) the whole point of inla.stack is to join things together with NA:s in the required places, so NA:s in there is expected.
2) both stacks have three column data matrices where the same two last columns are completely full of NA in both stacks. If you run a multi-likelihood model I would expect that to be a problem, as there would be no data whatsoever. If you only have one likelihood, use a vector instead.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another crash problem
messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel and Finn

My stack is part of larger 3-likelihood model. I run only the first likelihood to check if it is ok. There are also spatial indices in this stack that are not used for the model here. They are invoked in other models. On purpose I construct the stacks general so that they apply to several models. This simplifies modeling and will hopefully reduce the number of mistakes.

In all cases the simple model has been running smoothly except for this large case, which is not even accepted by inla. Hence, your explanation does not seem to apply, Finn. Actually, a slightly different program of same size with a different index (which actually is not even used in the model) runs smoothly.

I am inclined to think that I have exceeded some internal limits of the stack program by writing a stack command beyond what you conceive sensible persons to do. If so, I would like to know what these limits are.

best
Øyvind

As a programmer I appreciate such events as they may point to errorscan of cou
